### Problem: Maximum Gap {#sec-srt-p3-b}

::: {.p-statement}
An integer array `nums` ($1 \le n \le 10^5$, $0 \le \mathit{nums}[i] \le 10^9$). Return the **maximum difference between two successive elements in the sorted array**; return $0$ if $n < 2$. LC requires a **linear-time**, linear-extra-space algorithm — a plain sort is $O(n\log n)$ and only a stepping stone.

Source: [LC 164 · Maximum Gap](https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-gap/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}

Example: `nums = [3,6,9,1]` → sorted $[1,3,6,9]$, successive gaps $2,3,3$ → answer $3$. `nums = [10]` → $0$.
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
The answer is a gap between neighbours *in sorted order*, so the naive route sorts. But the values span $10^9$ — far too wide to count (@sec-srt-p3-a's histogram is out). Bucket sort's insight rescues it. The $n-1$ successive gaps add up to $\max - \min$, so (an averaging, or pigeonhole, argument) the largest of them is *at least* $\lceil (\max-\min)/(n-1) \rceil$. Cut $[\min, \max]$ into buckets of width $w = \max(1, \lfloor (\max-\min)/(n-1) \rfloor)$, which is at most that bound. Two values in the same bucket differ by at most $w - 1$, so no within-bucket pair can be the answer, and the true gap always lies **between** two buckets. That means each bucket only needs its min and max (2 numbers), and one scan of the non-empty buckets' seams gives the answer in $O(n)$.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Test every pair for ``successive in sorted order``.** For each ordered pair $(x, y)$ with $x < y$, check whether any other value $z$ satisfies $x < z < y$; if none does, $(x, y)$ is a successive pair of the sorted array and their difference $y - x$ is a candidate gap. Take the maximum. $O(n^3)$ time with the naive inner check — the direct transcription of the definition.
2. **Sort, then scan neighbours.** `b = sorted(nums)`; answer $= \max (b[i+1] - b[i])$. $O(n\log n)$ — the reference oracle LC disallows as the final word but that proves the bucket answer.
3. **Bucket / pigeonhole, linear.** Put each value in bucket $\lfloor (\mathit{nums}[i]-\min)/\text{width} \rfloor$ keeping only per-bucket min and max. The maximum gap is the largest difference between a non-empty bucket's min and the previous non-empty bucket's max. $O(n)$ time, $O(n)$ space.

**Invariant.** With $\text{width} = \max(1, \lfloor (\max-\min)/(n-1) \rfloor)$ and $\lfloor (\max-\min)/\text{width} \rfloor + 1$ buckets, the answer is $\ge \text{width}$ while any within-bucket difference is $\le \text{width} - 1$; so the maximum successive difference joins the max of one non-empty bucket to the min of the next non-empty bucket, and the seam scan sees every such pair.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Test every pair for ``successive in sorted order``

::: {.form-next}
The definition, verbatim. Walk every ordered pair $(x, y)$ with $x < y$; declare it *successive* iff no other element $z$ falls strictly between them, i.e. $x < z < y$ is empty. The maximum successive-pair difference *is* the maximum gap. $O(n^3)$ time with a fresh linear scan for each pair — cubic work that any hint of sortedness could collapse, but nothing about sorting is used yet.

**Worked example.** `nums = [3, 6, 9, 1]`. Ordered pairs with $x < y$: $(1, 3), (1, 6), (1, 9), (3, 6), (3, 9), (6, 9)$. Test each for a $z$ strictly inside: $(1,3)$ none $\to$ successive, gap $2$; $(1,6)$ $3$ is inside $\to$ skip; $(1,9)$ both $3, 6$ inside $\to$ skip; $(3,6)$ none inside $\to$ successive, gap $3$; $(3,9)$ $6$ inside $\to$ skip; $(6,9)$ none inside $\to$ successive, gap $3$. Maximum $= 3$. Three successive pairs, one maximum — the answer LC wants, without any $O(n\log n)$ or $O(n)$ trick.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def gap_pair_brute(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    if n < 2:
        return 0
    best = 0
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            if i == j or nums[i] >= nums[j]:
                continue
            x, y = nums[i], nums[j]
            if any(x < z < y for z in nums):        # something in between: not successive
                continue
            best = max(best, y - x)
    return best
```

##### C++

```cpp
// fragment - all-pairs successive-pair oracle
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;
int maxGapBrute(const vector<int>& a) {
    int n = (int)a.size();
    if (n < 2) return 0;
    int best = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j) {
            if (i == j || a[i] >= a[j]) continue;
            int x = a[i], y = a[j];
            bool inside = false;
            for (int k = 0; k < n; ++k)
                if (x < a[k] && a[k] < y) { inside = true; break; }
            if (!inside) best = max(best, y - x);
        }
    return best;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The outer loops pick every ordered index pair; `nums[i] >= nums[j]` skips the pairs that are not $x < y$. `if any(x < z < y for z in nums)` is the *successive* test — if any value falls strictly between, this pair is not adjacent in the sorted array. `best = max(best, y - x)` keeps the largest difference over all successive pairs. $O(n^2)$ pairs times $O(n)$ inner test = $O(n^3)$ total — the price of refusing to sort.

#### Sort, then scan neighbours

::: {.form-next}
Sort and take the biggest adjacent difference. $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(n)$ space — LC wants linear, but this is the *definition* restated as an algorithm and the oracle we test the bucket pass against; it also reuses @sec-srt-p1 exactly. Compared to the pair scan, one $O(n\log n)$ sort removes the entire $O(n^3)$ ``is this pair successive?`` test.

**Worked example.** `nums = [3, 6, 9, 1]` sorted to $[1, 3, 6, 9]$; gaps $2, 3, 3$; maximum $3$.
:::

##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-0164-sort
def gap_sort(nums):
    if len(nums) < 2:
        return 0
    b = sorted(nums)
    return max(b[i + 1] - b[i] for i in range(len(b) - 1))

for _ in range(300):
    nums = [random.randint(0, 200) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 16))]
    assert gap_sort(nums) == gap_pair_brute(nums)
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int maxGapSort(vector<int> a) {
    if (a.size() < 2) return 0;
    sort(a.begin(), a.end());
    int best = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i < (int)a.size(); ++i) best = max(best, a[i] - a[i - 1]);
    return best;
}

int main() { vector<int> v{3, 6, 9, 1}; maxGapSort(v); }
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `if len(nums) < 2: return 0` handles the single/empty guard LC states explicitly. `b = sorted(nums)` then `max(b[i+1] - b[i] ...)` is the @sec-srt-p1 neighbour scan: after sorting, the largest successive gap is by definition between two neighbours, so no non-adjacent pair needs checking.

#### Bucket (pigeonhole): only per-bucket min and max

::: {.form-next}
The linear algorithm LC demands. Scatter values into equal-width buckets by their position in $[\min, \max]$, keep just each bucket's min and max, and the answer is a seam between non-empty buckets — never inside one. $O(n)$ time, $O(n)$ space.

**The averaging argument, in plain words.** Walk the sorted values from $\min$ to $\max$: you take $n-1$ steps that together cover $\max - \min$, so at least one step is as long as the average, $(\max - \min)/(n-1)$, rounded up. The bucket width was chosen no larger than that average, and two values in the same bucket are less than one width apart. So the biggest step can never stay inside one bucket: it leaves some bucket at that bucket's **max** and lands in a later bucket at its **min**, with only empty buckets between. That is why each bucket needs only its two extremes. (Often some bucket is empty and the big step jumps over it, as in the example below, but the argument does not need an empty bucket: for $[1, 2, 3, 4]$ every bucket of width $1$ is full and the answer $1$ is still a seam.)

**Worked example.** `nums = [3, 6, 9, 1]`: $\min=1$, $\max=9$, $n=4$, width $=\max(1, \lfloor 8/3 \rfloor)=2$, buckets $=\lfloor 8/2\rfloor+1=5$. Value→bucket: $1{\to}0, 3{\to}1, 6{\to}2, 9{\to}4$ — bucket $3$ is empty, and the step $6 \to 9$ jumps over it. Bucket mins $[1,3,6,-,9]$, maxs $[1,3,6,-,9]$. Seams: $3-1=2$, $6-3=3$, $9-6=3$; maximum $\boxed{3}$.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-0164-bucket
def gap_bucket(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    if n < 2:
        return 0
    mn, mx = min(nums), max(nums)
    if mn == mx:
        return 0
    width = max(1, (mx - mn) // (n - 1))
    nb = (mx - mn) // width + 1
    bmin = [math.inf] * nb
    bmax = [-math.inf] * nb
    for x in nums:
        i = (x - mn) // width
        if x < bmin[i]:
            bmin[i] = x
        if x > bmax[i]:
            bmax[i] = x
    gap, prev = 0, bmax[0]                 # bucket 0 holds mn, so it is non-empty
    for b in range(1, nb):
        if bmin[b] == math.inf:             # empty bucket: skip, seam grows
            continue
        gap = max(gap, int(bmin[b] - prev))
        prev = bmax[b]
    return gap

for _ in range(300):
    nums = [random.randint(0, 200) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 16))]
    assert gap_bucket(nums) == gap_sort(nums)
assert gap_bucket([3, 6, 9, 1]) == 3                     # LC example; the board sample
assert gap_bucket([10]) == 0                             # single element
assert gap_bucket([1, 1, 1, 1]) == 0                     # all equal
assert gap_bucket([1, 1000000]) == 999999                # extreme span
assert gap_bucket([1, 2, 3, 4]) == 1                     # no empty bucket at all
assert gap_bucket([0, 10 ** 9]) == 10 ** 9               # full value range
print("gap_bucket OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <climits>
using namespace std;

int maximumGap(vector<int>& nums) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    if (n < 2) return 0;
    int mn = *min_element(nums.begin(), nums.end());
    int mx = *max_element(nums.begin(), nums.end());
    if (mn == mx) return 0;
    int width = max(1, (mx - mn) / (n - 1));
    int nb = (mx - mn) / width + 1;
    vector<int> bmin(nb, INT_MAX), bmax(nb, INT_MIN);
    for (int x : nums) {
        int i = (x - mn) / width;
        bmin[i] = min(bmin[i], x);
        bmax[i] = max(bmax[i], x);
    }
    int gap = 0, prev = bmax[0];
    for (int b = 1; b < nb; ++b) {
        if (bmin[b] == INT_MAX) continue;   // empty bucket
        gap = max(gap, bmin[b] - prev);
        prev = bmax[b];
    }
    return gap;
}

int main() { vector<int> v{3, 6, 9, 1}; maximumGap(v); }
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `width = max(1, (mx-mn)//(n-1))` is the bucket size; the `max(1, ...)` guard prevents a zero width when all values crowd together, and the `mn == mx` early-return already handled the fully-equal case. `nb = (mx-mn)//width + 1` makes every value from `mn` to `mx` fall into some bucket; it is below $2n$, so the arrays stay $O(n)$. `bmin`/`bmax` hold only two numbers per bucket — the whole memory trick. The final scan skips empty buckets (`bmin[b] == math.inf`) and measures each seam `bmin[b] - prev` against the previous non-empty bucket's max `prev`. Because the max gap always joins one bucket's max to the next non-empty bucket's min, this seam scan never misses it, and it never measures a within-bucket span.
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**All-pairs ``successive?`` test** is $O(n^3)$ time with the fresh inner scan ($O(n^2)$ if you precompute sortedness once). **Sort + scan** is $O(n\log n)$ time — the middle rung hands the ``is this pair successive?`` question to sortedness itself, since adjacency in a sorted array is exactly ``successive in sorted order``. **Bucket** is $O(n)$ time and $O(n)$ space — one scatter pass, one seam pass, fewer than $2n$ buckets — meeting LC's linear requirement. It is *not* counting sort: the value range is $10^9$, so no histogram is possible; the buckets are keyed by *position in $[\min,\max]$*, not by value, which is what keeps it linear (@sec-srt-p3-a explains why counting sort fails here).
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $n < 2$: return $0$ before touching buckets.
- All equal ($\min = \max$): return $0$; otherwise `width` and `nb` degenerate.
- Two elements: width $= \max - \min$, the seam is that difference — correct.
- Never compute a within-bucket max gap and think it counts: the averaging bound says the answer is always at a seam, so per bucket you only store min and max.
- `width` must be at most the average gap; using $\lceil (\max-\min)/(n-1) \rceil$ as the width can put the answer inside one bucket.
:::

::: {.practice}
- [LC 220 · Contains Duplicate III](https://leetcode.com/problems/contains-duplicate-iii/){difficulty="Hard"} — buckets of width $t+1$: a close pair is in the same or a neighbouring bucket.
- [LC 347 · Top K Frequent Elements](https://leetcode.com/problems/top-k-frequent-elements/){difficulty="Medium"} — bucket by frequency (at most $n$) to beat a full sort.
:::
